items.title: The Barber's Dilemma
items.question: In a village, the barber shaves exactly those men who do not shave themselves. Who shaves the barber?
choices: He is bald, so the question is void
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Either way the rule breaks: if he shaves himself he violates it, and if he doesn't he must shave himself. Russell built this in 1901 to break set theory.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — every 'practical' answer quietly breaks the rule. If he shaves himself, he's shaving someone who shaves himself. If someone else shaves him, then he doesn't shave himself — so by the rule he must shave himself. The premise is self-contradictory; that's the point.
items.lessonContent:
Russell's paradox arrives from harmless-looking self-reference: a set that contains all sets that don't contain themselves.
The village version dresses the same trap in everyday clothing — a rule that applies to itself.
Logicians built type theory to fence off exactly this kind of loop.
Spotting self-reference early is a core reasoning skill.
Share this: try writing a sentence that describes itself and see where it bites.

items.title: Quantum Spookiness
items.question: Quantum entanglement means measuring one particle instantly influences its entangled partner, no matter the distance — and this cannot be used to send faster-than-light messages.
items.correctExplanation: True — proven by the 2022 Nobel experiments. The correlation is instant but each individual result is random, so no information travels.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Einstein called it 'spooky action at a distance' and doubted it, but experiments settled it. The catch people miss: the results are random, so entanglement can't carry a message faster than light.
items.lessonContent:
Einstein's 'spooky action' nickname came from discomfort with what the mathematics predicted.
Entanglement correlations have passed every Bell test since the 1970s.
Randomness at each end is what blocks faster-than-light messaging.
The observer effect is a different phenomenon from entanglement — a common mix-up.
Share this: ask someone why entanglement can't send messages and enjoy the pause.

items.title: The More You Take
items.question: The more you take, the more you leave behind. What am I?
items.hintText:
Think about movement, not objects.
It's something you 'take' with your body.
You leave them behind you as you walk.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! Every step you 'take' leaves a footprint behind — the double meaning of 'take' is the whole trick.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is footsteps. The riddle plays on two meanings of 'take': taking a step versus taking an object. The more steps you take, the more you leave behind you.
items.lessonContent:
Wordplay riddles hide their trick in the double meanings of ordinary verbs.
The fair ones keep every needed clue inside the riddle itself.
Riddles older than a thousand years survive in the Exeter Book — the habit of riddling runs deep in human culture.
Reading a riddle twice, slowly, is the standard technique.
Share this: ask someone the oldest riddle you know and watch them reason it aloud.
